planting.note: Set container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil with afternoon shade; this Taiwanese high-elevation species tolerates more cold than many camellia species and smothers itself in small fragrant white flowers from late winter into spring.

directions: Choose a sheltered woodland-edge site with dappled light and acidic, free-draining soil before planting container-grown stock. Water deeply through the first two seasons to establish the fibrous root system, then taper off except during drought. Mulch with pine bark or leaf litter to keep roots cool and conserve moisture, and avoid heavy fertilizer that can push soft growth vulnerable to late frost. Prune only lightly right after the winter-to-spring bloom to maintain its naturally dense, upright habit.

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil with shelter from drying wind; this Hong Kong forest species develops showy cinnamon-colored peeling bark and needs protection from hard freezes.

directions: Site this small tree where its flaking, warm-toned bark can be seen in winter light, ideally against an evergreen backdrop. Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, especially while the thick leathery leaves are establishing on young plants. Large woody seed capsules follow the solitary white winter flowers and can be left on the plant for ornamental interest or removed to redirect energy to growth. This species is considered vulnerable in its native range, making garden and arboretum cultivation valuable for ex-situ conservation.
sources: International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List assessment

planting.note: Set out in spring in acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; this wide-ranging Himalayan species flowers in autumn and winter and has long been harvested regionally for its oil-rich seed.

directions: Grow in sheltered, humus-rich soil that mimics the understory conditions of its native Himalayan foothill forests. Fragrant white flowers appear from autumn into winter on older wood, so prune only after bloom to avoid sacrificing the next season's display. Seedpods mature slowly and have traditional value for pressed oil in parts of its native range, though most gardeners grow it purely for the late-season flowers and glossy foliage. Protect from prolonged hard freezes and strong drying wind.
sources: Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) species account
Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this old-world species, the type for the genus, is tough, drought-tolerant once settled, and lines its arching stems with small white flower clusters in mid-spring.

directions: Plant in any ordinary garden soil with good drainage; this steppe-and-woodland native from southeastern Europe through Siberia and the western Himalaya shrugs off heat, cold, and neglect once roots are established. Dense clusters of small white flowers wreathe the previous year's wood in mid-spring, so prune for shape immediately after flowering rather than in fall or winter. Established plants need only occasional supplemental water during extended drought. Its fine, blue-green summer foliage and twiggy winter silhouette make it a useful low-maintenance background shrub.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)

planting.note: Set out in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this vigorous central and southern Chinese species, introduced to Western gardens by plant collector E. H. Wilson, bears flat white corymbs along gracefully arching branches in early summer.

directions: Give this large, fountain-shaped shrub room to display its long arching canes, which bow under rows of flat-topped white flower clusters in early summer. It performs best in evenly moist, well-drained soil and full sun, though it tolerates part shade with a slightly looser habit. Renew older, less productive canes at the base every few years rather than shearing, since flowers form on growth from the prior season. It is sturdy enough for naturalized borders or large shrub plantings where its scale and old-China provenance can be appreciated.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)

planting.note: Set out in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this western Chinese species forms a graceful, slightly more compact mound than its relative S. veitchii, covered in flattened white flower clusters in early summer.

directions: Plant where the arching, wand-like stems can cascade freely, such as along a slope or border edge, in well-drained soil and full sun for the densest flowering. Clusters of small white flowers line the previous year's wood in early summer, so thin out the oldest canes right after bloom rather than cutting the whole plant back hard. It tolerates average garden soil and short dry spells once established but colors and flowers best with consistent moisture through spring. Use it as a specimen or massed as an informal flowering hedge.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)

planting.note: Set out in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this high-elevation Himalayan, southeast Tibetan, and northern Myanmar species carries grey-downy young foliage and dense rounded clusters of small white flowers in summer.

directions: Plant in lean, fast-draining soil and full sun to mimic the rocky mountain slopes this species calls home. The grey-felted new growth gives way to clean green leaves by summer, when rounded white flower clusters crowd the branch tips. It needs little supplemental water once roots are established and resents heavy, poorly drained soils more than cold. Lightly thin congested stems after flowering to keep the mounded habit open and tidy.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)
